summary: Describes the Simple Network Time Protocol (SNTP), a simpler adaptation of NTP for synchronizing computer clocks over the Internet. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 2030 and RFC 4330.

eli5.summary: A simple way for a computer to ask another computer what time it is and fix its own clock.

questions: when should i use sntp instead of ntp
what is the sntp message format
subtitle: A simpler way to synchronize computer clocks over the Internet.

tldr.problem: The full Network Time Protocol (NTP) is complex and requires significant computational resources. Many applications need clock synchronization but not NTP's precision and reliability mechanisms.
tldr.mechanism: SNTP simplifies NTP by removing state management and complex algorithms, operating as a stateless remote procedure call where clients request the current time and servers reply with a single timestamp.
tldr.outcome: SNTP provides easier clock synchronization for simpler systems and devices, but the full accuracy and reliability of NTP are not guaranteed. It has been superseded by RFC 2030 and RFC 4330.

today: RFC 2030 and RFC 4330 have superseded RFC 1769 with updated specifications for SNTP. Implementations should use the later RFCs for authoritative guidance.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SNTP (Simple Network Time Protocol) is a simplified adaptation of the Network Time Protocol (NTP) designed for applications that need to synchronize computer clocks but do not require NTP's full complexity. While the standard NTP includes sophisticated algorithms for handling multiple time sources, adjusting for network delays, and maintaining high accuracy, many systems only need basic clock synchronization to within a fraction of a second.

SNTP removes NTP's state management and complex algorithms, operating instead as a stateless remote procedure call (RPC) similar to the simpler UDP TIME protocol. This makes SNTP suitable for devices with limited resources or applications where millisecond-level accuracy is not required. The RFC recommends that SNTP be used only at the extremities of the synchronization network—clients should be at the leaves (furthest from the root) and servers should operate only at the root with a reliable external time source like a radio clock.
sections.eli5: SNTP lets a computer ask another computer for the current time and update its own clock. It is much simpler than the full NTP but works fine when you do not need perfect accuracy.

sections.title: Operating Modes
sections.content:
SNTP supports two modes of operation: unicast (point-to-point) and broadcast (point-to-multipoint). In unicast mode, a client sends a request to a server and receives a reply with the current time. In broadcast mode, a server periodically sends time messages to a designated broadcast address or multicast group, and clients listen without sending requests.

Broadcast mode can use either IP broadcast addresses, which are limited to a single subnet, or IP multicast addresses (such as 224.0.1.1), which can reach across networks. The RFC notes a security vulnerability: SNTP multicast clients can be disrupted by misbehaving or hostile servers anywhere on the Internet using the same multicast group address. To mitigate this, access control based on server source address or MD5-encrypted message authentication can be used.
sections.eli5: SNTP can work two ways: a client can ask a server for the time (like calling someone), or a server can broadcast the time to everyone listening (like announcing it on a loudspeaker).

sections.title: Message Format
sections.content:
SNTP uses the standard NTP message format, which begins with a header followed by optional authentication data. The message includes timestamps in NTP's special 64-bit format, where the first 32 bits represent seconds since 0h on 1 January 1900, and the last 32 bits represent the fractional part. This format provides precision of about 200 picoseconds.

The header fields include the Leap Indicator (warning of an upcoming leap second), Version Number, Mode, Stratum (clock hierarchy level), Poll Interval, Precision, Root Delay, Root Dispersion, and Reference Identifier. In SNTP, most of these fields are initialized with pre-specified values. The key field for SNTP clients is the Transmit Timestamp, which contains the server's current time of day. If this field is zero, the message should be disregarded as the server has not synchronized or never been synchronized to a valid time source within the last 24 hours.
sections.eli5: The SNTP message is like a postcard with the sender's address, the receiver's address, the message size, and most importantly, a timestamp showing what time it is.

sections.title: Client and Server Operations
sections.content:
An SNTP unicast client initializes an SNTP message with all fields set to zero except the first octet, where the Leap Indicator is set to 0 (no warning) and the Mode field is set to 3 (client). It then sends this to a server. When the reply arrives, the client extracts the time of day from the Transmit Timestamp field. To calculate the network propagation delay and local clock offset, the client can use the four timestamps: Originate (T1, when the request was sent), Receive (T2, when the server received it), Transmit (T3, when the server sent the reply), and Destination (T4, when the client received the reply).

An SNTP server receives a request message and modifies certain fields in the NTP header before returning the message to the sender. In unicast mode, the Version Number and Poll fields are copied from the request. The Mode field is set to 4 (server) if the request was in client mode. The Stratum field is set to 1 if the server is synchronized to a primary time source (such as a radio clock), or 0 if unsynchronized. The Leap Indicator is set to 0 for normal operation or 3 for unsynchronized. Timestamp fields are set with the current time, with the Originate Timestamp copied from the request to prevent replay attacks.
sections.eli5: A client sends a message asking for the time with a timestamp of when it sent the request. The server writes down when it received the request and when it is sending the reply, then includes the current time. The client can use these four timestamps to figure out the clock difference between them.

sections.title: UDP Port and Protocol Assignment
sections.content:
SNTP is implemented as a client of the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), which itself is a client of the Internet Protocol (IP). The UDP port number assigned to both NTP and SNTP is port 123, which is used in both the Source Port and Destination Port fields in the UDP header. This standardized port assignment allows SNTP clients and servers to use the well-known port for time synchronization services.

The UDP port 123 assignment means that both NTP and SNTP services can coexist and interoperate on the same network. An SNTP client can connect to either an NTP or SNTP server using the same port, and the servers will respond with their current time using the standard NTP message format. This compatibility simplifies deployment and allows simpler SNTP implementations to obtain time from more robust full NTP servers when needed.
sections.eli5: SNTP messages are sent using the same UDP port (123) that NTP uses. This means an SNTP client can get the time from either a simple SNTP server or a full NTP server.

sections.title: Status and Successors
sections.content:
RFC 1769 is an Informational document that supersedes RFC 1361 of the same title. The earlier version lacked details on broadcast mode operation and contained some typographical errors that were corrected in this version. However, RFC 1769 itself has been obsoleted by RFC 2030 and RFC 4330, which provide updated specifications for SNTP.

While SNTP remains a useful concept for simple time synchronization scenarios, implementations should prefer the later RFCs, which incorporate improvements and updated guidance based on operational experience with SNTP in various deployment contexts.
sections.eli5: This document explains SNTP, but it was later replaced by two newer documents (RFC 2030 and RFC 4330) that have better information.

fields.name: LI, VN, Mode
fields.desc: Leap Indicator (2 bits), Version (3 bits), Mode (3 bits).

fields.name: Poll Interval
fields.desc: Maximum interval between messages, as power of 2 in seconds.

fields.name: Precision
fields.desc: Clock precision, as power of 2 in seconds.

fields.name: Root Delay
fields.desc: Roundtrip delay to primary reference source.

fields.name: Root Dispersion
fields.desc: Nominal error relative to primary reference source.

fields.name: Reference Identifier
fields.desc: Identification of reference clock (e.g., ATOM, GPS, or IP address).

fields.name: Transmit Timestamp
fields.desc: Time server sent reply (T3); the server time of day.

messages.label: Request (Mode 3)
messages.note: Client sends time request with Originate Timestamp (T1)

messages.label: Reply (Mode 4)
messages.note: Server returns with Transmit Timestamp (T3) and Receive Timestamp (T2)
